The Master of the Boundless drank in silence and did not respond. The next day, Shi Chengqi saw him again and said:

"Yesterday I had a barb against you. Today my heart is just now rectified. What is the reason for this?" The Master said, "As for those clever and knowing, and those holy and sacred, I myself consider myself removed from them. Yesterday you called me an ox, and so I was called an ox. You called me a horse, and so I was called a horse. If one truly has the substance, then the name given by others is received; if one does not receive it, one then twice receives its harm. I wear it, always wear it. I do not wear it so that I may be wearing a garment." Shi Chengqi walked with his breast forward, avoiding his own shadow, and trod onward.

<summary>The Master of the Boundless, likely Zhuangzi's Laozi, remains silent when criticized, then explains that accepting or rejecting names given by others — even "ox" or "horse" — is a matter of substance and non-attachment. Shi Chengqi's heart is rectified, yet he walks away in a posture of defensive avoidance, still carrying the shadow of the Master's teaching.</summary>

<margin>Su's Commentary</margin>One who does not know the Way but pursues learning, his knowledge and experience increase daily, yet he lacks a unifying principle; inevitably this becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, choose the good and follow it; see much, and remember it; this is secondary knowledge." If one day he knows the Way, then he sees that what he previously held as true is but falsehood, and there is nothing which is not delusion. To abandon delusion and return to the original nature, this is called "reduction." Confucius said to Ziyi: "Do you think me to be one who learns much and remembers it?" He replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, it is not. I thread my teachings with a single unifying principle." Now, to forget the mind in order to purify and restore one's nature—this is what is meant by reduction. Yet if traces of delusion still remain, they persist together with their forgetting. It is through this complete purification of the mind to the state of restored nature, leaving no remainder, that one may then act spontaneously without losing the state of non-doing. People all desire to grasp the world and understand the principles of all matters, so they create affairs and seek after them. When this mind manifests externally, things resist it, and thus the goal is difficult to attain. The sage, having no aims, undertakes no affairs. When his mind manifests externally, things find peace in it. Although he does not seek to grasp the world's affairs and manage them, the world's affairs naturally order themselves and find peace.

<margin>Lü's Commentary</margin>Those who engage in learning have not yet heard the Way. Not yet having heard the Way, they must seek it, and cannot avoid being broad; therefore it is said to be "daily increase." Those who engage in the Way have already heard the Way. Having heard the Way and acting in accordance with it, they cannot avoid non-action; therefore it is said to be "daily reduction." To reduce yet further is still to risk remaining within the realm of action. It is necessary to reduce even the act of reducing itself, and only then does one attain non-doing. Non-doing is the state of tranquil stillness, without movement. "Nothing undone" is the state of responsive awareness, penetrating all principles of the world. This is what is meant by the <term>jingxue</term> <gloss>learning of the classics</gloss> non-anxiety and the divine. The divine is the realm of the Way. Who can attain this divine state? From this perspective, it is clear that to grasp the world, one must rely on non-doing, and that if one tries to use doing, it will be insufficient to grasp the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary</margin>Only when one knows all things can one speak of learning; thus learning seeks daily increase. Only when one can do all things can one speak of the Way; thus the Way seeks daily reduction. Yet while increase can be pursued through effort, reduction may be difficult to achieve through force. Only one who is supremely clear can suddenly cast off attachments and fall into the realm of non-doing, and thus can achieve all things without ceasing, applying limitless power to the world with effortless ease.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary</margin>Engaging in learning is for the sake of knowledge, thus it increases daily. Engaging in the Way is for the sake of abandoning delusion, thus it decreases daily. If knowledge is not perfected, then reduction is not complete; thus the daily increase is the foundation for the daily reduction. When reduction is applied again and again, and delusion is cast off and truth fully restored, then one attains non-doing. Having reached non-doing, all actions become as if not-doing—this is not something that can be discussed in terms of increase and reduction. When the state of non-doing is perfected, even the multiplicity of the world is unified by a single thread. If one tries to act upon affairs, then one affair will entangle and trouble the next; even a single object can become a snare, so how much less could one handle the multiplicity of the world?

The sage has no fixed mind, but makes the mind of the people his mind. The good I treat as good; the not-good I also treat as good—this is the virtue of goodness. The trustworthy I treat as trustworthy; the not-trustworthy I also treat as trustworthy—this is the virtue of trustworthiness. The sage, dwelling among the people, is dim and obscure, and makes the world's mind unified and whole. The people all fix their eyes and ears upon the sage.

There must be no beast's heart <note>i.e., bestial nature</note>; even if one has a beast's heart, if the appearance is similar, one will be regarded as kin. Those that bear horns, wear fangs, have spreading claws, fly aloft, or crawl on the ground are called birds and beasts. They are not necessarily without a human heart <note>i.e., human nature</note>; even if they have a human heart, if the appearance is different, they will be regarded as distant. The Yellow Emperor, the Serpent Goddess Nüwa, the Divine Farmer Shennong, and the Xia Emperor Yu: these had serpent bodies, human faces, ox heads, or tiger noses — they had non-human forms yet possessed the virtue of great sages. The Xia emperor Jie, the Shang emperor Zhou, King Lu Huan, and King Chu Mu: their appearances, with all seven orifices, were entirely identical to humans, yet they possessed the heart of birds and beasts. The common run of people cling to a single form in seeking the highest wisdom, but this is not the way to attain it. When the Yellow Emperor fought the Flame Emperor at the Wild Plain of Banquan, he arrayed bears, brown bears, wolves, leopards, <term>豼貅</term> <gloss>mythical beasts, here probably real wild carnivores or totemic animals</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, and used carrion birds, goshawks, eagles, and kites as his banners. This is one who used force to command birds and beasts. Yao commanded <term>夔</term> <gloss>Kui, a mythical or historical musician</gloss> to oversee music: striking the stone, rubbing the stone, all the hundred beasts danced in rhythm. With the ninefold completion of the <term>簫韶</term> <gloss>the Sublime Music of the Reed Pipes</gloss>, the phoenix came and made its perch.

<summary>This passage from the Liezi argues that outward form does not determine inner virtue or nature: legendary sage-emperors had non-human features, while depraved rulers appeared fully human. It also recounts ancient examples of commanding animals through force and music, illustrating themes of appearance versus reality and the relationship between humanity and the animal world.</summary>

Of old, the Son of Heaven had a thousand offices and the various lords had a hundred offices, because with these thousand offices the commands could reach throughout the lands of the Xia states, and this was called being king; with these hundred offices the commands could reach throughout the borders of one’s own state, and even if the state were unsettled, it would not come to ruin or fall to others<note>reading 遂 as “to fall” – meaning the ruin of one’s enterprise</note>, and this was called being a ruler. The child of a sacred king, or the descendant of one who possessed the realm, the holder of the dynastic register, the head of the ancestral house of the realm: yet if he lacked ability and was not upright<note>不中 means not correct, not proper</note>, then within his own borders the common people would resent him, and beyond them the various lords would rebel against him; near at hand the realm within his borders would not be unified, far away the various lords would not heed his commands; his orders would not be enforced within his own borders, and moreover the various lords would encroach upon and attack him. If this came to pass, then even though he had not been destroyed, I would say that he no longer possessed the realm. When the sacred king has passed away and the holder of the dynastic register is weak and unfit for office, and is not sufficient to unite<note>罷 (pronounced pī, meaning weak, unfit for duty; 縣 meaning to bind or unite</note> the realm, then the realm has no ruler. Among the various lords, if there is one who possesses virtue, a brilliant reputation, and authority, so that all the people within the seas desire to accept him as both ruler and teacher, and yet a tyrannical state alone is extravagant and unrestrained<note>暴國 refers to tyrants like Jie and Zhou; 獨侈 means exclusively self-indulgent and unrestrained; 安 here functions like “then”</note>, [he] must punish it, and must not harm the innocent people. To punish the ruler of a tyrannical state is like punishing a solitary man<note>獨夫 describes one whom no one under heaven supports, isolated like a single man</note>. If this can be done, then it can be called being able to use the realm. Being able to use the realm is what is meant by king. Tang and Wu did not seize the realm; they cultivated the Way, practiced righteousness, shared benefits with all under heaven, eliminated harms shared by all under heaven, and the realm came to them. Jie and Zhou did not lose the realm; they turned against the virtue of Yu and Tang, confused the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, practiced deeds of beasts, and accumulated their cruelty, and the realm<note>言天下自去也 – meaning the realm abandoned them of its own accord</note> departed from them.

<summary>This passage defines true kingship as founded on virtue and effective administration rather than hereditary right. A ruler who fails to govern well loses moral authority and his realm is considered “without a ruler”; the virtuous lord who restores order is the true king. Tang and Wu are praised not as usurpers but as restorers of righteous order, while tyrants like Jie and Zhou are condemned as having lost the realm through their own depravity.</summary>
<keywords>Xunzi, Correcting Standards, kingship, hereditary rule, virtue versus tyranny, Tang, Wu, Jie, Zhou, punishment of tyrants, benefit of the people, ritual and righteousness</keywords>

Therefore, one should not cling to the teaching, nor should one cling to what is not the teaching. For this reason, the Tathāgata often says: "Monks, know that my teaching is like a raft; the teaching itself should be abandoned, how much more so what is not the teaching."

### Seventh Division: No Attainment and No Teaching

Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained the highest, perfect, complete awakening? Has the Tathāgata taught any teaching?

Subhūti said: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed teaching called the highest, perfect, complete awakening, nor is there any fixed teaching that the Tathāgata can teach. Why is this? The teachings spoken by the Tathāgata cannot be grasped, cannot be spoken, are not a teaching, and are not the absence of a teaching. How so? All noble and saintly ones differ based on the unconditioned teaching <note>that is, the teaching of non-activity or non-striving, the ultimate truth beyond conditioned phenomena</note>.

### Eighth Division: The Teaching Arises from the Teaching

Subhūti, what do you think? If a person were to fill the entire universe of three thousand great world systems with seven kinds of precious jewels and give them as a gift, would the merit gained by that person be great?

Subhūti said: Very great, World-Honored One. Why is this? This merit is not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathāgata speaks of merit as great.

If another person were to receive and uphold even just a four-line verse from this scripture and teach it to others, their merit would be superior. Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and the Dharma of the highest, perfect, complete awakening of all Buddhas arise from this scripture. Subhūti, what is called the Buddha-dharma is not the Buddha-dharma <note>the teaching is provisional, not the ultimate truth</note>.

Wheat is the grain that bridges the interrupted and extends the depleted. In the summer season, the old grain has already been exhausted, and the new grain has not yet been harvested. The people, at this time, suffer from a lack of food. Wheat is the first to ripen, and thus it was considered important. Dong Zhongshu said: "In the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, other grains are not recorded when they fail to appear, but when there is 'no wheat and no millet' it is recorded. From this one can see that among the five grains, the sage placed the greatest importance on wheat and millet." For this reason, he persuaded Emperor Wu of the Han to promote the planting of wheat in the Guanzhong region. The *Monthly Ordinances of the Hall of Light* also contains a text promoting the planting of wheat in mid-autumn, and it is beyond doubt that whoever missed the planting season would be punished. All of this is because wheat is what people rely upon to bridge the gap, and they feared the people would not take it seriously.
